items.title: Equilibrium doesn't mean nothing is happening
items.claim: A reversible reaction at equilibrium has constant concentrations of reactants and products. People assume this means the reaction has stopped. It hasn't — forward and backward reactions are both still going at equal rates.
items.prompt: What is the evidence that equilibrium is dynamic, not static?

options.text: Isotopic labelling — add radioactive atoms to one side of an equilibrium and they appear on the other side over time, even though concentrations don't change
Equilibrium is in fact static — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Consider N2O4 in equilibrium with 2 NO2. Add a sample where one nitrogen is N-15 (a heavier isotope). At equilibrium the labelled atoms scramble — the heavy nitrogen appears in both N2O4 and NO2 even though their concentrations remain unchanged.

This only makes sense if the molecules continue to convert: N2O4 dissociates to 2 NO2 and recombines back continuously. At equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal, so net concentration changes are zero — but individual molecules undergo conversion many times per second.

The same idea applies to biological steady states: tissue protein levels can be constant while individual molecules are synthesised and degraded continuously.
items.why: Equilibrium sounds like cessation. The chemistry never stops — it just balances on a dynamic knife edge.

items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: Gases mix even when nothing energetic is gained
items.claim: Open a perfume bottle in still air. The fragrance fills the room. There is essentially zero enthalpy change — no heat is released. Yet the mixing is utterly spontaneous and would NEVER reverse on its own.
items.prompt: What drives mixing with no energy reward?

options.text: Entropy of mixing: vastly more microstates have the perfume molecules spread through the room than concentrated near the bottle; the system follows the overwhelming statistical odds

items.reveal:
For two ideal gases mixing at constant T and P, ΔH ≈ 0. But ΔS = -nR(x1 ln x1 + x2 ln x2), always positive when x1 and x2 are both non-zero. Gibbs free energy ΔG = ΔH - TΔS is therefore negative, and mixing is spontaneous.

The perfume could in principle un-mix into the bottle. The probability is roughly 1 in 10 to the (10 to the 23) — for practical purposes, zero. The second law is a statistical statement, not an absolute prohibition.

This logic underpins every observation that systems 'tend to disorder': cards left in a deck, gases filling containers, hot bodies cooling. Pure entropy with no enthalpy change is enough to drive the process firmly forward.
items.why: Spontaneity is often taught as 'releases energy'. Pure entropy of mixing — with no heat — drives transformations all by itself.
